analysis: Would bar the state and all political subdivisions from (1) imposing a tax or fee based on miles a person travels in a motor vehicle and (2) monitoring or limiting miles traveled unless the person voluntarily consents. Exceptions: interstate commercial vehicles under an interstate fuel-tax or registration agreement, and vehicles owned and operated by the state or a political subdivision.
arguments_note: 39 arguments filed for, 5 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
effective_date: Per measure text in pamphlet: effective 'if approved by the voters and on proclamation of the Governor.'
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure.
no_means: Keeps the current constitutional language on taxation.
title: Taxation - prohibits taxes or fees based on vehicle miles traveled and laws monitoring or limiting vehicle miles traveled without consent
type: Legislative referral - constitutional amendment (adds Ariz. Const. Art. IX, Sec. 26)
yes_means: Amends the Arizona Constitution to prohibit (1) taxes or fees based on motor vehicle miles traveled and (2) laws or rules that monitor or limit miles traveled without consent. These prohibitions do not apply in certain cases to interstate commercial vehicles or to vehicles owned by state or local governments.

analysis: Would bar the state, cities, counties, universities, community colleges, school districts and other subdivisions from preferential treatment or discrimination based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education or contracting, including where a federal program is involved. Would ban compelled statements supporting certain race-based DEI concepts, required confessions of privilege and related mandatory training. Would bar public funds for offices or positions that promote race- or ethnicity-based preferences, and bar disciplinary policies that differ by race or ethnicity. Specified exceptions apply.
arguments_note: 7 arguments filed for, 16 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure.
no_means: Keeps the current constitutional prohibition against preferential treatment or discrimination by the state based on race, ethnicity, or other classes.
title: Prohibition of Preferential Treatment and Discrimination - adds further details to the constitutional prohibition against preferential treatment or discrimination by the state based on race, ethnicity, or other classes
type: Legislative referral - constitutional amendment (amends Ariz. Const. Art. II, Sec. 36)
yes_means: Amends the current constitutional ban on state preferential treatment or discrimination to specifically prohibit: (1) requiring people to support race- or ethnicity-based preferential treatment or discrimination as a condition of education, employment or contracts; (2) spending public money on public-education positions responsible for promoting such treatment; and (3) disciplinary practices that treat students or employees differently by race or ethnicity. This includes requiring or asking for statements supporting race-based diversity, equity and inclusion, with exceptions for health services, legal and other reasons.

analysis: Reaffirms that only U.S. citizens may register and vote. Voters would present valid government-issued proof of identity in each election, as prescribed by law, and could choose to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on Election Day. Foreign nationals could not contribute or spend to influence Arizona elections. Election laws, including early and mail voting, would be valid if rationally connected to a legitimate state interest. The Legislature must appropriate implementation costs. Applies to elections on or after Jan. 1, 2028.
arguments_note: 26 arguments filed for, 35 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
effective_date: Legislative Council analysis: applies 'to all elections that take place on or after January 1, 2028.'
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure. The measure itself requires the Legislature to appropriate the money needed to implement it.
no_means: Keeps the current constitutional provisions governing elections.
title: Election Requirements - requires all voters, including voters who vote by mail, to show government-issued ID to vote in each election; makes other changes to election administration and campaign finance prohibitions
type: Legislative referral - constitutional amendment (adds Ariz. Const. Art. VII, Sec. 19)
yes_means: Amends the Arizona Constitution to: (1) require proof of identity in each election, including when voting by mail; (2) limit acceptable documentation to government-issued ID; (3) require officials to give all voters the option to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on Election Day; (4) prohibit foreign nationals from contributing or spending to influence Arizona elections, and prohibit knowingly accepting such money; (5) create a new standard for judicial review of election laws, which may make them harder to challenge; and (6) require the Legislature to fund implementation.

analysis: Restricts city, town and other local taxes on food for home consumption. Jurisdictions that had approved such a tax by Jan. 1, 2025 could raise it only with voter approval, and only up to 2% of the tax base, with no increase if the rate is already 2% or more. Jurisdictions without such a tax would need voter approval to adopt one, also capped at 2%. All adoptions and increases are barred between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.
arguments_note: 1 arguments filed for, 3 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
effective_date: Ballot language: the retroactive prohibition covers July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2027. A general effective date was not stated in the sources read.
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure.
no_means: Keeps the current laws on local government taxation.
title: Municipal Transaction Privilege Tax - retroactively prohibits local governments from adopting or increasing a tax on groceries without voter approval and sets a maximum rate of 2%
yes_means: (1) Retroactively bars local governments from adopting or increasing a grocery tax from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2027. (2) After that, local governments could adopt or raise a grocery tax only with voter approval, and any new or increased rate would be capped at 2%.

analysis: Declares drug cartels (associations engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking for profit or terrorism) to be terrorist organizations. Requires AZDOHS to use 'all lawful means available within its authority' against them. States the measure does not support an alien's asylum claim under federal law.
arguments_note: 1 arguments filed for, 1 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure.
no_means: Keeps the current laws on terrorism and the Arizona Department of Homeland Security.
title: Arizona Department of Homeland Security - declares that drug cartels are terrorist organizations; directs the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to do everything in its authority to address drug cartels
yes_means: Declares drug cartels to be terrorist organizations and directs the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to do everything in its authority to address cartel threats. Defines 'drug cartel' as an ongoing association engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking or terrorism under Arizona law, and states that the measure does not support an alien's asylum claim.

analysis: Bars males from female interscholastic and intramural teams, using the sex on the athlete's original birth certificate. Requires teams to be designated male, female, coed or mixed. Bars public and private schools, colleges and athletic associations from allowing use of restrooms, locker rooms or showers not designated for a person's birth-recorded sex. Expands who can sue or be sued. Titled the 'Protect Girls' Sports in Arizona Act.'
arguments_note: 17 arguments filed for, 37 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure.
no_means: Keeps the current laws on student athletics.
title: Student Athletics - requires all schools and athletic associations to designate athletic teams as male, female, or coed based on the biological sex of the athletes as defined at birth; prohibits these entities from authorizing use of private spaces not designated for a person's sex
yes_means: (1) Requires private schools, public schools and athletic associations to designate every team as male, female or coed/mixed by sex and to keep males off female teams. Current law applies this only to public schools and those competing against them. (2) Bars schools and associations from letting anyone use private spaces such as restrooms not designated for that person's sex. (3) Defines 'sex' as biological status recorded at birth on the original birth certificate. (4) Lets athletes sue schools and associations that knowingly violate the law.

analysis: Bars photo enforcement for speeding or traffic-control-device violations unless the agency signed a contract before Dec. 31, 2026. A local authority with a contract needs voter approval at the next general election to continue. If voters reject it, the system must stop within 90 days. Approval lasts 10 years and must be renewed by voters.
arguments_note: 4 arguments filed for, 6 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
effective_date: Ballot language uses a Dec. 31, 2026 contract cutoff. A general effective date was not stated in the sources read.
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure.
no_means: Keeps the current laws on photo enforcement systems.
title: Photo Enforcement Systems - prohibits state agencies and local governments from using photo enforcement systems for traffic enforcement unless provided by contract as of December 31, 2026; requires local governments to obtain voter approval to continue their use
type: Legislative referral - statute (amends A.R.S. 28-1201; adds A.R.S. 28-1207)
yes_means: (1) Bars state agencies and local governments from using photo enforcement to identify traffic violators unless they contract for those systems by Dec. 31, 2026. (2) Local governments must get voter approval of existing systems at the next regular general election, and again every 10 years, to keep using them.

analysis: Covered districts must spend at least 60% of operational spending on direct instruction. Starting in FY 2027-28, districts below that level must raise the share by at least 0.5 percentage point a year. Non-compliant districts lose 25% of their Classroom Site Fund allocation per year of non-compliance, up to 100% after four years, unless waived. Withheld money goes to compliant districts.
arguments_note: 2 arguments filed for, 28 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
effective_date: Legislative Council analysis: the annual spending-increase requirement begins in fiscal year 2027-2028. A general effective date was not stated.
fiscal_note: None. JLBC says its 300-word fiscal impact summary requirement 'excludes legislatively referred propositions' (azjlbc.gov/?p=330), and no fiscal statement was found for this measure. Per Legislative Council, money withheld from non-compliant districts is reallocated to compliant districts the following year.
no_means: Keeps the current laws on school district budgets.
title: School District Budgets - requires certain school districts to spend at least sixty percent of their operational spending on direct instructional expenses as defined by the Auditor General; reduces certain state funding for non-compliant districts
yes_means: (1) Districts with 7,500+ students, or operating in a county of 500,000+ people, must spend at least 60% of operational spending on direct instruction. (2) The Auditor General defines the terms. (3) Non-compliant districts must adjust spending each year until they comply. (4) The Department of Education cuts Classroom Site Fund money to non-compliant districts by 25% per year, subject to limited waivers from the Superintendent.

arguments_note: 10 arguments filed for, 0 against (approximate counts). Arguments are written by supporters and opponents and are not official analysis.
effective_date: Collection begins the month after the existing jail tax (A.R.S. 42-6109.01) expires (March 2027) and may continue for no more than 20 years (A.R.S. 42-6109.02(C)).
fiscal_impact: County resolution: 'It is estimated that the total annual taxes generated will approximate $313 million' for July 2027-June 2028 (first full fiscal year), growing about 4.7% a year. Collections from March 2007 through Nov. 2025 totaled $3,254,764,452. JLBC fiscal note on SB 1144 (2025): the tax generated $279 million in FY 2024; a 0.2% extension 'would generate $324 million in FY 2028'; if it expires, county revenues fall about $323.9 million in FY 2028; 'no state fiscal impact.' The statute also requires a county maintenance-of-effort payment from the general fund.
no_means: Rejects the $0.002 jail sales tax. The existing jail tax still expires in March 2027.
title: County Jails: Transaction Privilege Tax of One-Fifth of One Cent
type: County referral (Board of Supervisors resolution under A.R.S. 42-6109.02) - countywide sales/excise tax continuation
yes_means: Approves a county sales tax of one-fifth of one cent ($0.002) for county jail facilities and programs: the same rate as the existing jail facilities excise tax, which expires in March 2027. It starts the month after the current tax expires and may run up to 20 years.

fiscal_impact: Official pamphlet: 'The issuance of these bonds will result in a property tax increase sufficient to pay the annual debt service on bonds.' Average additional rate is $0.3771 per $100 of assessed value. Estimated cost for a $250,000 owner-occupied home is $121.86 a year for ten years ($1,218.62 total). Total cost is $160,717,778 ($136,000,000 principal plus $24,717,778 interest). Maximum interest is 8.00%, with maturities of 1 to 20 years. Separately, the district's informational page says there would be 'NO INCREASE in the secondary property tax rate' if assessed values stay at least at current levels (2026 rate $0.85 per $100).

title: Gilbert Unified School District No. 41 - School Improvement Bonds ($136,000,000)
type: School district bond authorization (special election, Nov. 3, 2026)
yes_means: Authorizes the Governing Board to issue and sell $136,000,000 of school improvement bonds, repaid with secondary property taxes, for renovation and construction, buses, grounds, furniture, equipment, technology and related costs.
appears_on: Voters who live in Gilbert Public Schools
